title: Sum 1 to N (Recursion)
directAnswer: Base case `n == 0` returns 0; else return `n + sum(n-1)`. Closed form n(n+1)/2 avoids recursion entirely.

remember.takeaway: Recursion mirrors the math, but a closed form may beat it.
antiSignals: Large n — use the loop or formula

problemStatement: Given a non-negative integer `n`, compute `1 + 2 + … + n` recursively.
understanding: sum(n) = n + sum(n-1), bottoming out at sum(0) = 0.

approaches.name: Linear recursion
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
sum(n) = n + sum(n−1), bottoming out at sum(0) = 0 — the base-plus-shrink recursion applied to addition.

**Why it mirrors the math.** The definition reads exactly like the recurrence: the sum up to n is n plus the sum up to n−1. Each call peels off one term until it reaches the empty sum, 0.

**Why recursion is the *wrong* tool at scale.** Each call adds a stack frame, so this is O(n) stack depth; for n = 10⁵ that risks a stack overflow. The iterative loop is O(1) space, and the closed form n(n+1)/2 is O(1) time — both beat the recursion. Saying so shows judgement.

**Tail-call note.** Some languages optimise tail recursion to O(1) stack; Java and CPython do not, so the depth concern is real there.
hints: Express the sum to n in terms of the sum to n−1.
Is recursion the best tool here, given large n?
approaches.insight: Mentioning the O(1) closed form shows you know recursion isn't always the right tool.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n nested calls, each O(1) work, with an O(n)-deep stack.

edgeCases.behavior: Deep recursion risks stack overflow — prefer loop/formula.

pitfalls: Deep recursion blowing the stack for large n.

commonMistakes: Deep recursion blowing the stack for large n.
patternNote: A core fresher pattern: Base case + shrink. Master it on small inputs and it transfers to harder problems.
